title: Mendelssohn's Torah Commentary
summary: A commentary on the Torah in which Fridental participated.

enrichment.markdown:
**The commentary and its collaborators.** The strongest outside evidence is bibliographical, not biographical. A digitized 1778 pamphlet describes the project behind Mendelssohn’s German Pentateuch translation and commentary, and includes sample pages from Numbers. A separate digitized title page identifies *Netivot ha-Shalom* as Mendelssohn’s Torah commentary, printed in Berlin around 1783. ([commons.wikimedia.org](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAlim_litrufah.pdf?utm_source=openai))

- The name **Aharon ben-Zekharia Fridental** does not appear in the outside material I located under *Fridental*, *Fridental/Fridenthal*, or *Aaron/Aharon* paired with Yaroslav/Jarosław. That leaves his identification with the commentary’s contributor uncertain.
- A reference article identifies **Aaron of Jarosław** as the commentator on Numbers for the project, alongside other contributors to different books of the Torah. This makes him a possible match for the person in the record, but does not establish that he was Aharon ben-Zekharia Fridental. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biurists?utm_source=openai))
- **Moses Mendelssohn** is firmly linked to the project: the outside references describe the translation and commentary as a collaborative work, rather than a commentary written entirely by him. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Mendelssohn?utm_source=openai))

**Yaroslav, Berlin, and the broader setting.** The spelling *Jarosław* appears in the outside reference for Aaron’s contribution; it does not by itself confirm the person’s birthplace or residence. The Berlin title-page evidence anchors the printed work there. I found no reliable outside record connecting Fridental personally to **Bohemia, Moravia, Germany**, or the **Lviv Teacher Seminary**. The records located do not establish a biographical link between the commentary’s collaborators and the Lviv institution. ([commons.wikimedia.org](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AMendelssohn_Or_LiNtiva.JPG?utm_source=openai))

**Lviv community and related works.** Lviv had a long-established Jewish community, and the city became a major Jewish cultural center; that is useful context for why a book about Lviv might remember a scholar through his participation in a German-Hebrew biblical project, but it does not prove Fridental’s personal ties to any particular synagogue or institution. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv_during_the_Middle_Ages?utm_source=openai)) I found no source in the permitted archives connecting the named **Commentary on Numbers** or **Millot ha-Higayon of Maimonides** to Fridental beyond the supplied record.

**Search limits.** I searched the permitted Yad Vashem, USHMM, YIVO, JewishGen, Arolsen, Geni, Wikipedia, and Wikimedia Commons domains using Fridental/Fridenthal and Aaron/Aharon with Yaroslav/Jarosław, plus Mendelssohn, Numbers, and the named Lviv seminary. The searches did not yield a securely identifiable Fridental biography or family record. The positive findings above come from Wikimedia Commons and Wikipedia; absence from these searches should not be taken as evidence that no such records exist.
